2. Detect cycles (A→B→C→A) and peel chains (descending amounts hop-by-hop) in the counterparty graph.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: Neutral — 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting may be implicated, but the facts do not establish that a covered financial institution detected a reportable “suspicious transaction” or that any SAR-filing obligation was triggered.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates Treasury regulations requiring a “financial institution” to report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” and provides a safe harbor and confidentiality for such reports. Element-by-element: (1) Covered reporter: § 5318(g) applies to a “financial institution” (as defined/covered by BSA and implementing rules), but the fact pattern describes an individual customer (SYN_2dae4781) and transactions; it does not identify the involved bank/MSB/broker-dealer or other covered institution, so it is unclear whether a § 5318(g) reporter exists. (2) Suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation: the data show many small ACH/card/wire/cheque transactions and a “high” risk rating with expected monthly volume ~$1,366, but there is no information indicating the transactions are linked to a possible violation (e.g., structuring, fraud, money laundering, sanctions evasion) or that they meet regulatory SAR thresholds; § 5318(g) itself does not specify dollar thresholds without the implementing regulations. (3) Trigger/duty to file: because the statute’s duty is implemented “under regulations prescribed by the Secretary,” and the facts do not state that the institution detected suspicious activity under those rules or failed to file, applicability cannot be determined. Contiguous phrase in answer and here: “31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting”.
